newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian Metals -- Aluminium perks up after LME tumble.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals -- Aluminium perks up after LME tumble.

text.p: Japanese buying of aluminium picked up this week after a tumble in London Metal Exchange prices to within striking distance of fresh two-year lows, although volumes were modest, traders said on Wednesday.
They also said spot market premiums continued their gradual recent slide in the aftermath of negotiations on premiums for fourth-quarter contracts.
"This always happens after the premium negotiations," one trade house source said.
Talks last month between Japanese traders and Western producers set premiums for the October-December quarter around $62 a tonne over LME cash prices, market sources said.
One said the softer premiums may also reflect excessive recent buying by trade houses.

Traders said the latest drop in LME prices encouraged modest end-user buying, although enthusiasm was dulled by a continued weakening in the yen, which on Wednesday broke above 110 yen to the dollar for the first time since mid-July.
LME three-month aluminium slid Tuesday to $1,455 a tonne, barely holding above a two-year low of $1,454 hit on July 15. In early London trading on Wednesday, aluminium was quoted at $1,458/60.

Market sources said many base metal end-users continued to buy on a hand-to-mouth basis, which one user attributed to uncertainty about Japan's economic outlook, although more buying for the fourth quarter was expected to emerge if LME aluminium prices slid further to $1,440-$1,450.

Traders said the fourth quarter was also a slow demand period, especially for can sheet, although extrusion business was termed brisk as housing demand remained strong ahead of next April's scheduled rise in Japan's consumption tax.
Premiums in the copper market also eased modestly, due in part to a seasonal drop in air conditioner production and expectations that scrap supplies would soon hit the market, traders said.
The ending of a water shortage at the large Onahama smelter without any production cutbacks was also said to have eased worries about tight supplies.

One trade house source added, however, that availability of domestically refined copper may remain tight through the end of this year, due in part to low inventories at some refineries after strong demand over the summer.

Regarding recent news that Thailand will slash its import tariffs on copper cathode to 1.0 percent from the current 6.0 percent through the end of December 1998, traders said they expected this to boost Thai imports of cathode, although little impact was foreseen on supplies in the region as a whole.

The zinc market remained quiet, with premiums on Chinese metal for delivery to Japan remaining too high, at $90 to $100 a tonne over LME cash prices, to interest users in Japan's sluggish domestic market, traders said.
